newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS - Siemens expands list of divestment targets.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Siemens expands list of divestment targets.

text.p: German industrial conglomerate Siemens AG said on Wednesday it was maintaining its forecast for flat profit this year even though overseas sales and orders boomed in the first half of 1996/97.
Siemens sales for that period rose six percent to 44.7 billion marks ($26.1 billion), as an 11 percent rise in overseas sales offset a two percent decline in German sales.
But the company said it now planned to divest more non-core businesses over the next year or so than it had expected only two months ago.

Siemens expected to sell or put into joint ventures businesses with annual sales totaling about 5.5 billion marks -- up from an earlier target of businesses totalling more than three billion in sales.
"We are following a strategy to strengthen our portfolio," spokesman Thomas Weber told Reuters. "It is a process that continues -- buying and selling."
Traders were selling Siemens shares on Wednesday, as the stock closed floor trading at 88.90 marks, down 2.30, while the blue-chip DAX index rose 55.62 points to 3,395.95.

Bayerische Vereinsbank AG analyst Peter Thilo Hasler said the market was disappointed that Siemens did not budge from its November prediction of no profit increase for the business year ending September 30.

Orders in the period rose 11 percent to 48.6 billion marks, with the international portion climbing 20 percent and German orders falling three percent. Favourable currency rates boosted international orders by two percentage points, Siemens said.

Strong growth came in Siemens' public communicaitons unit, a maker of equipment for phone companies. Its first-half sales rose 31 percent to 6.3 billion marks. The private networks unit, which makes mobile, cordless and standard telephones, saw sales rise 30 percent to 4.9 billion marks.
Although semiconductor prices have halted their slump of last year, Seimens chip sales fell two percent in the first half to 2.3 billion marks.
Weber said Siemens was cautious about the chip business. "Prices are stable, but it's too early to say if this is a trend," he said. "They could fall again."

In transport systems, where Seimens makes locomotives and mass transit systems, first-half sales fell 11 percent to 1.6 billion marks, while power generation sales dropped 28 percent to 2.4 billion marks.
Hasler said Siemens "can't move fast enough" to unload weaker businesses, although he added the company was on track to see profit begin climbing again in 1997/98.
"We have the company rated 'outperform'," Hasler said. "We see the shares rising to over 100 marks next year."
Hasler said said restructuring in the transportation and medical divisions, which are expected to show losses this year, would return to profitability in 1997/98.

Transport systems, which makes locomotives and mass transit systems, was in the midst of a transition from analogue to digital technology and under pressure from international competition, Weber said.
Medical technology was looking for a buyer or joint venture partner for a dental equipment business that has a sales volume of about one billion marks, he said.

The dental business and Siemens' 1.6 billion mark defense electronic group, which has been on the block since March, would bring the volume of expected divestments to about 5.5 billion marks, Weber said.
In February chief executive Heinrich von Pierer said the company sought sell-offs or joint ventures for businesses with sales volume of three billion to 3.5 billion marks.
"We want to accomplish this over the next 12 months or so," Weber said. "It is partly realised. We have no time problem."
($ = 1.713 German Marks)
